standard.title: Compare language structures using metalanguage
standard.description: compare and explain similarities and differences between Chinese and English language structures and features, using familiar metalanguage
standard.prior_knowledge: Students entering at Y7-8 have intuitive grammatical knowledge of the target language from home use, and English grammar knowledge from schooling. They have not previously been asked to compare the two systems analytically, name grammatical features using metalanguage, or examine text-type conventions across languages.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students compare and explain similarities and differences between the target language and English language structures and features, using familiar metalanguage across text types and grammatical categories.

nodes.label: Metalanguage for grammatical comparison
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use metalanguage to describe grammatical features in both the target language and English, and compare how specific features function across the two languages.
nodes.minimum_width: Use at least five metalanguage terms correctly in comparing at least two grammatical features across target language and English.
nodes.typical_width: Use metalanguage in target language or English for grammatical description — nouns, verbs, adjectives, subject, predicate; compare grammatical features including word order, tense expression, and adjectival verb constructions; discuss aspects of grammar across both languages.
wider: Create a bilingual metalanguage comparison resource — explaining a specific grammatical contrast to a student learning one of the two languages
Investigate a grammatical feature that works fundamentally differently in the two languages — explain what communicative function it serves and how the other language handles the same need
nodes.hinge_reason: Metalanguage for grammatical comparison is the prerequisite for all analytical language work. Entry students with strong intuitive grammar but no analytical framework cannot describe, compare or explain language features — which is the core demand of this descriptor.

response_modes.reason: Grammatical comparison requires students to hold two systems in mind and reason about structural differences. Explicit metalanguage instruction followed by systematic category-by-category comparison builds this analytical capacity.

success_criteria: Uses at least five metalanguage terms correctly
Compares at least two grammatical features across target language and English with accurate explanation

nodes.label: Text-type and sequencing comparison
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare how different text types sequence and develop ideas in the target language and English, identifying structural and language feature differences.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare the structure of at least one text type (e.g. blog, email, argument, report) across target language and English, identifying at least three differences.
nodes.typical_width: Compare different ways of sequencing ideas for different audiences and purposes; compare blog versus email conventions; compare argument structure in speech versus essay; read formal target language texts and compare with everyday speech; compare traditional and contemporary literary expressions.
wider: Analyse how argument structure differs across target language and English texts — identify where the writer's position appears, how evidence is organised, and discuss the cultural logic behind the difference
Create the same text type in both languages, then compare the structural and language choices made — identify what is transferred and what is adapted

response_modes.reason: Text-type comparison must be applied across varied genres before students can generalise their comparative analytical capacity. Single-genre comparison produces narrow analytical skills that don't transfer.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Entry students who already use both languages have direct access to comparative text experience. Width investment here — making this implicit cross-language awareness explicit and analytical — develops a bilingual analytical lens that is a distinctive competence of this learner group.
success_criteria: Compares the structure of at least one text type across target language and English
Identifies at least three structural or language feature differences

nodes.label: Teaching and applying comparative knowledge
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can apply comparative language knowledge to access unfamiliar content and explain key language differences to others.
nodes.minimum_width: Apply comparative knowledge to access at least one unfamiliar text, and produce at least one explanation or resource about a key language difference for a peer or younger learner.
nodes.typical_width: Apply understanding of text and language features to access unfamiliar content; read texts and select appealing expressions to explain their choices; apply knowledge of formal text features to understand news articles and reports; explain key language differences using support resources.
wider: Create a teaching resource about a specific language difference — test it with a real or simulated learner audience and revise based on feedback
Apply comparative linguistic knowledge to analyse a genuinely unfamiliar text type — document the strategies used and evaluate their effectiveness

response_modes.reason: Teaching and applying comparative knowledge integrates metalanguage (node 1) and text-type comparison (node 2) into a transfer task. The teaching investment is in creating genuine transfer conditions — real unfamiliar texts, real teaching audiences — that require functional application of comparative knowledge.

success_criteria: Applies comparative knowledge to access at least one unfamiliar text
Produces an explanation or resource about a key language difference for another learner
